summary: Read as a tired judge, Caplet's biggest communication problem is that the lines a reader will remember from IPS V5 are the wrong ones: the unsupported co-sponsor claim, 'never below the floor', 'cannot miss the range' and 'no dollar asset is safer'. The plainest true idea ('money she already owns rather than a forecast'; 'never promise money you don't own') sits in team notes, not in V5. Sentence-level readability is fine. V5 scores Flesch-Kincaid grade 10.7, plainer than Wharton's own IPS brief (15.9) and the case (13.7). The real load is concept density: about 18 rules, 7 distinct years and 5 dollar figures in 497 words, against the team's own cap of 12 ideas. So simplifying means cutting ideas, not shortening sentences. Last year's 'over-complex' lesson has moved backstage. The page now carries one strategy name instead of about six frameworks, but the AI kit the Final Report will draw on is full of internal jargon (RAB 2,206 mentions, p95 1,110, gate 1,055, REC 702). Applied to V5, the 16 Oct [AI] suggestions double the dollar figures (5 to 10) and add six shares and odds in four formats, which works against 'Keep the presentation simple' (IPS:101-102). The ladder-cost conflict is resolved: on the 15 Oct curve the ten payments cost $294,461 priced to payment dates (the number sheet) but $297,847-$298,628 priced to the maturities of the bonds Caplet owns (the lenses). Any claim about Caplet's plan should use the owned-bonds basis, dated, or the IPS should carry no figure. Other new points: 'facility floor' reads literally as a building floor; 'Caplet', 'cap' and 'floor' are names of interest-rate derivatives to a bond judge; the team's own draft checker misses V5's real jargon; Sydney dates in reflections will not match WInS's ET dates. The lens gives a four-line story test (problem, idea, proof, trade-off), a jargon blacklist with plain replacements, and twelve number rules.

findings.title: The lines a judge will remember from V5 are the wrong ones
findings.problem: A screening reader keeps one or two lines. In V5 the most quotable lines are the unsupported co-sponsor claim, 'never below the floor', 'cannot miss the range' and 'no dollar asset is safer'. Each is false or unsupported by Caplet's own numbers, so the judge's lasting impression is built on claims the team cannot defend. The true, simple idea (the bottom of the range is owned, not forecast; never promise money you don't own) is in team notes, not in V5.

findings.problem: To a fixed-income reader a caplet is one period of an interest-rate cap (an option, a derivative, and WInS bans derivatives), and 'cap' and 'floor' are names of interest-rate derivatives. V5 uses 'floor' 10 times and 'capped' once under a team named Caplet. 'Root and branch' means 'complete or thorough' (an overhaul), an odd label for a hold strategy. A credit specialist sat on the 2024-2026 finale panels. The team name is fixed; the strategy words are not.
